title: Utility Types
description: Use TypeScript's built-in type transformers to derive new types from existing ones without duplication.

challenges.title: What is Partial<T>?
challenges.whyMatters: Partial<T> is the most-used utility type — it appears in every update/patch function, form handler, and config merge you'll write.
hints: Partial makes every property optional by adding ?

choices.label: B)  { readonly host: string; readonly port: number }
C)  { host: string | null; port: number | null }

challenges.title: Partial — update function
challenges.description:
Define an interface `ServerConfig` with:
- `host` (string)
- `port` (number)
- `maxConnections` (number)
- `debug` (boolean)

Then write `updateConfig(config: ServerConfig, changes: Partial<ServerConfig>): ServerConfig` that merges changes into the existing config and returns the result.
challenges.whyMatters: Partial is the canonical type for patch/update operations — you only pass the fields that change, not the entire object.
hints: Partial<ServerConfig> makes every field optional
Spread both objects into a new object — properties from the second argument take precedence when the same key appears in both

challenges.title: Readonly — immutable config
challenges.description:
Define a `DatabaseConfig` interface with: `host`, `port` (number), `name`, `user`, `password` (all strings except port).

Write `freezeConfig(config: DatabaseConfig): Readonly<DatabaseConfig>` that returns the config as Readonly.

Write `describeConfig(config: Readonly<DatabaseConfig>): string` that returns `"user@host:port/name"`.
challenges.whyMatters: Readonly<T> prevents mutation at the type level — it's how you mark shared config objects as safe to pass around without defensive copying.
hints: Readonly<T> makes all properties readonly — TypeScript blocks assignment
Readonly<T> is a compile-time concept only — think about what the function body needs to do at runtime to return the config unchanged
Follow the output pattern from the description — four fields joined with @, :, and / as separators

challenges.title: Pick and Omit
challenges.description:
Define a `FullUser` interface with: `id` (string), `name` (string), `email` (string), `password` (string), `createdAt` (string), `role` (string).

Create two derived types using Pick and Omit:
- `PublicUser` = Pick keeping only: id, name, email, role
- `CreateUserDto` = Omit removing: id and createdAt

Write functions:
- `toPublic(user: FullUser): PublicUser`
- `describeUser(user: PublicUser): string` → `"name (role)"`
challenges.whyMatters: Pick and Omit let you derive API response shapes and DTO types from a single source model — the most common pattern in typed backends.
hints: Use Pick to select only the four fields that should be visible externally — list them as a union of string literals
Use Omit to exclude the two fields the server generates automatically — everything else stays required
toPublic only needs to return the four fields declared in PublicUser — pull them from the FullUser argument and return a new object

challenges.title: Record — typed dictionary
challenges.description:
Write a function `buildEnvMap(pairs: [string, string][]): Record<string, string>` that converts an array of key-value pairs into a Record.

Then write `getEnv(map: Record<string, string>, key: string, fallback: string): string` that returns the value for key, or fallback if the key is absent.
challenges.whyMatters: Record<K, V> is the typed equivalent of a plain JS object used as a dictionary — environment maps, HTTP headers, and config stores all use this pattern.
hints: JavaScript has a built-in that converts an array of key-value pairs directly into an object — use it on the pairs argument
Access the map by key — if the key is absent the result is undefined; use the nullish coalescing operator to fall back to the default

challenges.title: Required — enforce completeness
challenges.description:
Define an interface `PartialOptions` where all four fields are optional:
- `timeout?: number`
- `retries?: number`
- `baseUrl?: string`
- `debug?: boolean`

Write `withDefaults(options: PartialOptions): Required<PartialOptions>` that fills in defaults:
- timeout: 5000
- retries: 3
- baseUrl: "http://localhost"
- debug: false
challenges.whyMatters: Required<T> is useful as a return-type assertion — it documents that your function always returns a fully populated object, even if the input was sparse.
hints: Required<PartialOptions> strips all ? marks — every field is mandatory in the return type
Spread the defaults object first so provided options override them — the defaults object should list all four fields with their fallback values

challenges.title: ReturnType and Parameters
challenges.description:
Write a function `createServer(host: string, port: number, debug: boolean)` that returns `{ host, port, debug, start: () => string }` where start returns `"started"`.

Then write, using only ReturnType and Parameters (not manual types):
- `type Server` — the return type of createServer
- `type ServerArgs` — the parameter tuple of createServer
- `restart(server: Server, args: ServerArgs): Server` — creates a new server from the args
challenges.whyMatters: ReturnType and Parameters let you derive types from existing functions — so when the function changes, the derived types update automatically.
hints: Use ReturnType with typeof to derive the Server type directly from the function — no manual annotation needed
Use Parameters with typeof to capture the argument tuple of createServer — the result is a tuple of the three parameter types
Call createServer from inside restart and spread the args tuple so each element lines up with the matching parameter

challenges.title: Combining utility types
challenges.description:
Define a `Service` interface with: `id` (string), `name` (string), `endpoint` (string), `apiKey` (string), `timeout` (number, optional), `retries` (number, optional).

Derive:
- `PublicService` = Omit `apiKey` then make it Readonly
- `ServicePatch` = Partial of Omit of `id` and `apiKey` (fields you can update)

Write:
- `toPublic(s: Service): PublicService`
- `applyPatch(s: Service, patch: ServicePatch): Service`
challenges.whyMatters: Chaining utility types — Readonly<Omit<T, K>>, Partial<Omit<T, K>> — is the pattern behind every well-typed CRUD API you'll see in production codebases.
hints: Chain two utility types: first remove the sensitive field with Omit, then wrap the result in Readonly to prevent mutation
First omit the fields that must never be changed, then wrap the remainder in Partial so every update field becomes optional
Merge the original service with the patch — spread both into a new object, letting the patch override any matching fields

challenges.title: Bring it together
challenges.description:
Build a typed event system:

`interface EventMap { userCreated: { id: string; name: string }; orderPlaced: { orderId: string; total: number }; error: { code: number; message: string } }`

Write:
- `type EventName` = keyof EventMap
- `type EventPayload<K extends EventName>` = EventMap[K]
- `emit<K extends EventName>(event: K, payload: EventPayload<K>): string` → returns `"event:" + JSON.stringify(payload)`
- `on<K extends EventName>(event: K, handler: (payload: EventPayload<K>) => void): void` → calls handler immediately with payload
challenges.whyMatters: Typed event systems — using keyof + indexed access — are the pattern behind typed EventEmitters, message buses, and pub/sub systems in TypeScript.
hints: Derive EventName from EventMap without listing the keys manually — the keyof operator extracts all keys as a union
Use indexed access to look up the payload type for event K in EventMap — K acts as the index
Return a string that prefixes the event name with a colon, then appends the serialized payload
The on function receives both the handler and the payload — immediately invoke the handler with the payload
